claims.text: The initial materials are nanoparticles containing five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and crystallized as uniform single-phase solid solutions.
HEA nanoparticles whose constituent metals have similar melting points and diffusion kinetics will remain single-phase and chemically homogeneous throughout 473–1923 K exposure.
Large mismatches in constituent melting points or diffusion kinetics cause differential diffusion.
Differential diffusion drives elemental segregation and phase transformation in multielement alloy nanoparticles.
Diffusion kinetics are governed by the constituent metals' intrinsic melting points and diffusion activation barriers.
Similar melting points and diffusion barriers produce uniform or sluggish diffusion among the constituent metals.
Uniform or sluggish atomic diffusion maintains high configurational entropy.
High diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics inhibit atomic rearrangement and preserve a uniform elemental distribution during annealing.
Entropy-induced slow kinetics are a key source of thermal structural stability in multielement alloy nanoparticles.
Significant kinetic mismatches destabilize a homogeneous solid solution and promote phase segregation or localized ordering.
The matched-property nanoparticles will retain a uniform elemental distribution after high-temperature exposure.
The matched-property nanoparticles will retain a single-phase structure after exposure across 473–1923 K.
The mismatched-property nanoparticles will develop compositional gradients, elemental segregation, or secondary phases relative to their initial homogeneous state.
When oxidation and substrate interactions are minimized, inter-element diffusion disparities are the primary variable controlling stability across 473–1923 K.
Local lattice distortions and minor microstructural fluctuations may affect phase-segregation kinetics at the upper end of the temperature range.
Similar retention of chemical and phase homogeneity in both matched and mismatched sets would falsify the proposed dependence on melting-point and diffusion-kinetic matching.
Significant segregation or compositional inhomogeneity in the matched-property set would falsify the hypothesis.
